newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-HOLYFIELD BRUSHES OFF TYSON'S FEROCITY IN FAVOR OF GOD.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-HOLYFIELD BRUSHES OFF TYSON'S FEROCITY IN FAVOR OF GOD.

text.p: Mike Tyson's image as the Darth Vadar of a dark sport who once said he tries to punch nose bones into opponents' brains, has left more than a few fighters thinking last rites rather than left-rights before climbing into the ring.

The two most recent examples are putative champions Frank Bruno, who on the way into the ring last March crossed himself more times than a convent of nuns on Good Friday, and Bruce Seldon, who in September very quickly spied a soft spot to land and fell down from the breeze of one of Tyson's punches.
Evander Holyfield, though, is different. Very different.
Former champion Holyfield is glad that Tyson has said he wants to hurt him for some alleged slight.
"How many times Tyson say he wanna hurt somebody?" said Holyfield dismissively. "He said he was gonna hurt a lot of people and he performed. He beat people and turned around and hugged them.

"I want to beat the best guy," said Holyfield looking relaxed, even serene, in his suite at the MGM Grand Hotel. "I'm glad I'm the guy that he wants to hurt, so I'm sure he'll be at his best, so when I win they'll say, you know, I beat the guy at his best."

In the minds of many people, Saturday's scheduled 12-round bout -- which seems unlikely to go the distance -- is a fight between good and evil, with Holyfield the good guy in the struggle to take Tyson's World Boxing Association title.
It readily could be inferred that Holyfield believes that against Tyson he has a huge edge on his side -- God.

Asked directly if he thought God favoured him or if he was was David of the David and Goliath story he recounted as a way of showing the power of God, Holyfield said with a knowing smile, "I'm Evander."
Holyfield denied God was going to make his left hooks hurt more than Tyson's.

But in his insistent homages to God and his declarations of an iron-willed allegiance to his faith, Holyfield seemed to feel that when punch comes to punch the man with more faith will be able to draw on it when he needs it most.
"The Lord is within me. If you go out and do all that you can then the Lord will help you," said Holyfield, in the course of a long, rambling discourse on God and fighting.
"You can pray to some gods and some gods don't hear prayers but there's a God out there that do hear prayers.

"That's the one that you do need to be praying to that you can deliver yourself out of all these ups and downs," said Holyfield, whose words could be interpreted as referring to Tyson, who converted to Islam while serving three years in prison for rape.
The love of a career is paramount, Holyfield said.

"I can't tell what (Tyson) got into boxing for. I got into the game because I love what I'm doing, and what I love doing it shows in my performance. And with my performance I glorify God for giving me my health and strength," said Holyfield, wearing a red t-shirt that hugged his bulging muscles.
"If you go out and do all that you can then the Lord will help you."

Holyfield, who has earned well over $75 million in his career and will receive at least $11 million for Saturday's bout against Tyson, who will get $30 million, was asked why he still takes punches for a living.

"I'm doing it out of love. I'm doing it because this is what the Lord called me to do, and I'm going to do it, and I'm gonna do it well. And I'm gonna give him the glory and that glory is gonna touch a lot of people's lives and help people overcome a lot of obstacles in their life," Holyfield said.

In what could pass as a loud stage whisper to Tyson, Holyfield said: "Anytime you do something that don't please nobody but yourself what is it? You need to edify and uplift people not to destroy them.
"My whole thing is to show people what I have. My body is like this because I worked hard at it, I trained. My body didn't come out of a cracker box."

True to his professions of piety Holyfield said, "I still have a lot of compassion for Tyson. Even now I feel that the man has his share of ups and downs ... I'm just hoping he finds true peace, that when his career is over he don't have to suffer."
Holyfield also recounted his friendship with Tyson when both fighters were attempting to make the 1984 U.S. Olympic team.
Both young men were seen as outcasts by the other boxers. Tyson was seen as an ungainly, uncool 17-year-old and Holyfield was perceived as "a country boy who don't know nothing," he said.

"Tyson was one of them guys what you called real lovable guys that he looked for that affection, that loving ... success hit him so quickly, he didn't know who to trust," said Holyfield, certain these days about where to place his trust.
